transcript.text: Every so often when I use the hob the electrics in the house go off. Not every time, maybe once a week. It's an induction hob, Hisense I think.

An intermittent trip like that is fairly common with induction hobs, and the cause is usually one of a few things. The first step is to work out **which switch is tripping** in your consumer unit (fuse box).

## Step 1: Check what trips

Next time it happens, before you reset anything, look at which switch has dropped:

- **A big switch covering several circuits, often labelled "RCD" or with a "T" test button.** This means the RCD detected current leaking to earth. This is the most common case with induction hobs.
- **A single small switch just for the cooker/hob (an MCB).** This means the circuit drew too much current or there's a fault on that circuit.
- **An RCBO (single-width switch with its own test button).** This could be either cause.

If the whole house goes off, it's most likely the RCD or the main switch.

## Likely causes

**If it's the RCD:**
- **Wrong RCD type.** Induction hobs use electronics that can leak a small DC-type current. Older consumer units often have **Type AC** RCDs, which don't handle this well and can nuisance-trip. Modern regs require **Type A** (marked with a symbol showing a sine wave plus a pulsed wave). Swapping it is a straightforward job for an electrician.
- **Cumulative leakage.** Lots of appliances on the same RCD (fridge, washing machine, computers) each leak a little. When the hob adds its share, the total can tip it over. This explains "only sometimes."
- **Moisture.** Spills or steam getting into the hob, or a damp connection or back box behind it, can cause it.
- **A developing fault in the hob itself.**

**If it's the MCB:**
- **Overload.** Several zones on boost, especially with the oven on the same circuit, may exceed the breaker rating. Check the hob's required supply (often 32A) against the breaker.
- **Loose or burnt connection** at the cooker switch or terminal block. This is worth taking seriously because it can overheat.

## What you can do now

1. Note **which switch** trips and **what was on** at the time (which zones, boost, oven, kettle, washing machine).
2. See if there's a pattern, such as boost mode or the end of a wash cycle.
3. Look at the cooker isolator switch on the wall. **If it's discoloured, smells hot or buzzes, stop using the hob** until it's checked.
4. Don't keep resetting it and carrying on indefinitely without finding the cause.

## When to get help

I'd get a qualified electrician to look at it. They can test insulation resistance and RCD performance and check the connections in about an hour. In the UK, look for an NICEIC or NAPIT registered electrician. If the hob is still under warranty and the electrics check out fine, contact Hisense. The model number is usually on a sticker underneath the hob or in the manual.

If you let me know which switch trips and roughly how old your consumer unit is, I can help narrow it down further.

I think it's a big switch in the middle that drops, but I don't know if that's the RCD thing you mean. I've no idea how old the fuse box is. Once after it tripped there was a faint electrical smell, but nothing since.

That helps. A big switch in the middle that drops is very likely an **RCD**, but the **electrical smell** changes things.

## The smell

A faint electrical smell after a trip could point to a connection overheating or arcing, often at the cooker switch on the wall, the connection behind the hob, or inside the fuse box. It could also be harmless, such as a bit of spilled food burning on the hob, but you can't tell from here.

I'd recommend:
- **Getting an electrician out soon** rather than waiting to gather more evidence.
- Until then, **using the hob as little as possible**, and not while you're out or asleep.
- **Stopping using it completely and switching it off at the cooker switch** if you notice the smell again, any scorching, a warm or discoloured wall switch, or buzzing or crackling.
- Making sure you have a working smoke alarm, ideally a heat alarm in the kitchen.

## Telling whether it's an RCD

Look at the switch that drops:

- A small button marked **"T"** or **"Test"** means it's an RCD.
- Text like **"RCD"**, **"RCCB"**, **"30mA"** or **"IΔn 30mA"** also means it's an RCD.
- If it's labelled **"Main Switch"** with no test button, it's just an isolator, and those don't normally trip on their own. Mention that to the electrician.

Some fuse boxes have two RCDs, each covering half the house. If only some things go off, that fits too.

## Rough age clues

| What you see | Likely age |
|---|---|
| Metal casing | Probably 2016 or later |
| Plastic casing, one or two RCDs | Roughly 1990s to 2015 |
| Pull-out fuses with wire, no RCD | Very old, needs upgrading |
| A sticker with a date or electrician's details | Check it, it often gives the install or test date |

If the RCD has a symbol showing **just a wavy line (~)**, it's probably Type AC, which as I mentioned is prone to nuisance tripping with induction hobs.

## Telling the electrician

Give them this:
- Which switch trips and roughly how often (about once a week).
- That it happens when using the induction hob.
- That there was a faint electrical smell once after a trip.
- The hob make, and the model if you can find it.

They'll likely check the connections at the hob and cooker switch, run an insulation test, and check the RCD type and performance. With the smell involved, I wouldn't put this one off.

If you can take a photo of the fuse box, or read out any markings on that switch, I can help you work out what you've got.
